verses.translation: And there was given{H5414} to me one{H259} reed{H7070} in the likeness{H1823} of a staff{H4294}, and he said{H559}: Arise{H6965}! Measure{H4058} the sanctuary{H1964} of YHWH{H3068} and his altar{H4196}, and those who pray{H6419} in it.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הֵיכַל (heykal, H1964 — 'sanctuary/temple hall') paired with the Tetragrammaton: הַהֵיכַל יַהְוֶה ('the sanctuary of YHWH'). Greek has τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ ('the temple of God'). The Hebrew preserves the specific divine name YHWH where the Greek generically says 'God' (Θεός). A back-translator from Greek would write היכל אלהים ('sanctuary of God'), not 'sanctuary of YHWH.' The Tetragrammaton is untranslatable from a Greek source that lacks it.

Uses הַמִּתְפַּלְּלִים (hamitpalelim — 'those praying', Hithpael of פלל H6419). Greek has τοὺς προσκυνοῦντας ('those bowing/worshipping'). These are different religious activities. A back-translator from Greek would write המשתחוים (hamishtachavim — 'those bowing down/worshipping'), the standard Hebrew for proskyneō. The Hebrew author uses the rabbinic technical term for verbal prayer/intercession (hitpalel), not physical prostration.

Uses כִּדְמוּת (kidmut — 'in the likeness of', H1823). This is the prophetic vision formula from Ezekiel (Ezek 1:5, 1:10, 1:22, 1:26, 8:2, 10:1, 10:21-22). Greek has ὅμοιος ('similar to'). A translator from Greek could use כמו (kemo) or דומה (domeh). The Hebrew author naturally uses the Ezekielian vision vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ὁ ἄγγελος εἱστήκει λέγων ('the angel stood saying') — specifying an angel as the speaker. Hebrew has simply ואמר ('and he said') without identifying the speaker.
Greek: 'the temple of God' (τοῦ Θεοῦ). Hebrew: 'the sanctuary of YHWH' (יהוה). Different divine designation.
Greek: 'those worshipping' (προσκυνοῦντας — physical prostration). Hebrew: 'those praying' (מתפללים — verbal intercession).
translation_notes: 'Sanctuary' for heykal — the specific inner hall of the Temple (1 Kings 6:3,5,17), distinguishing it from the broader temple complex (bayit).
כִּדְמוּת (kidmut) is the same word used in Genesis 1:26 (בדמותנו — 'in our likeness') and throughout Ezekiel's visions. It carries stronger theological weight than a simple simile.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 40:3-5 — Ezekiel is given a measuring reed to measure the temple. The pattern of receiving a reed to measure sacred space is an Ezekiel motif. Both the Hebrew Revelation and Ezekiel use קנה (qaneh — 'reed') as the measuring instrument.

verses.translation: But the inner{H6442} sanctuary{H1964} — cast{H2236} it outside{H2351}, and do not measure{H4058} it, for it is given{H5414} to the peoples{H5971}. And they shall trample the holy{H6944} city{H5892} forty{H705}-two{H8147} months{H2320}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew says הַהֵיכָל הַפְּנִימִי ('the INNER sanctuary', H6442). Greek says τὴν αὐλὴν τὴν ἔξωθεν τοῦ ναοῦ ('the court which is OUTSIDE the temple'). These are OPPOSITE spatial references — inner vs. outer. No translator working from the Greek 'outer court' would write 'inner sanctuary.' The Hebrew author envisions the innermost sanctum itself being given over to the nations — a far more radical profanation than merely ceding the outer court. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the chapter.

Uses זְרוֹק (zeroq — 'cast/throw', imperative of zaraq H2236). In priestly Torah texts, zaraq is the technical verb for sprinkling sacrificial blood on the altar (Lev 1:5,11; Num 18:17; 2 Kings 16:13). Using the priestly sprinkling verb for an act of EXCLUSION from sacred space creates a profound irony that only a Hebrew author immersed in priestly vocabulary would produce.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'the inner sanctuary' (ההיכל הפנימי). Greek: 'the court outside the temple' (τὴν αὐλὴν τὴν ἔξωθεν τοῦ ναοῦ). Opposite spaces excluded from measurement.
Hebrew: ἔκβαλε ἔξω ('cast out') in Greek is a general verb. Hebrew uses zaraq — a priestly technical term.
contradictions: The inner/outer reversal between Hebrew and Greek represents a genuine theological divergence, not a translation variant. In the Hebrew vision, YHWH's withdrawn presence renders even the innermost sanctum available for profanation. In the Greek, only the outer (Gentile) court is given over. These are irreconcilable spatial theologies.
translation_notes: דָרְסוּ (darsu — 'they shall trample') is a later Hebrew/Aramaic verb not attested in the OT. No standard Strong's number. Greek πατήσουσι likewise means 'trample/tread.'
חֳדָשִׁים (chodashim, H2320) means both 'months' and 'new moons.' The root חדש carries the meaning 'new/renewal' — the liturgical calendar term.
textual_notes: Daniel 8:13-14 — 'How long shall the vision be... to give both the sanctuary and the host to be trampled underfoot?' The trampling of the holy city echoes Daniel's vision of the sanctuary's profanation.

verses.translation: And I{H589} give{H5414} my two{H8147} witnesses{H5707}, and they shall prophesy{H5012} a thousand{H505} and two{H8147} hundred{H3967} and sixty{H8346} days{H3117}, clothed{H3847} in sackcloth{H8242}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עֵדִים (edim — 'witnesses', H5707) — the specific Torah legal term. Deuteronomy 17:6 and 19:15 establish that 'at the mouth of TWO witnesses or THREE witnesses' a matter is confirmed. The phrase 'two witnesses' (שני עדים) directly invokes the Torah's evidentiary standard. Greek μάρτυσι ('witnesses/martyrs') is broader and later acquired the meaning 'martyr.' The Hebrew stays within Torah legal vocabulary.

Hebrew has present-tense נוֹתֵן (noten — 'I give/am giving'). Greek has future δώσω ('I will give'). The Hebrew participle presents the act as ongoing — God is continuously giving his witnesses. Greek places it in the future. These are different temporal perspectives a translator would not interchange.
greek_deviations: Greek adds an implied 'power/authority' (some MSS have ἐξουσίαν) — 'I will give [power] to my two witnesses.' Hebrew simply says 'I give my two witnesses' without the addition of power/authority.
Hebrew: present participle נוֹתֵן ('I give'). Greek: future indicative δώσω ('I will give'). Different tense.
translation_notes: 'Witnesses' for edim preserves the Torah legal-covenantal sense. These are not mere observers but covenant witnesses with legal standing under Torah.
1,260 days = 42 months = 3½ years — matching the 42 months of trampling in verse 2. The prophesying and the trampling are concurrent.
textual_notes: The two-witness requirement (Deut 19:15) governs all of Torah jurisprudence. God sends the minimum required number of covenant witnesses to render a legal verdict against the nations.

verses.translation: And these are the two{H8147} olives{H2132} and two{H8147} torches, standing{H5975} before{H6440} the Elohim{H430} of the earth{H776}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses אֲבוּקוֹת (avukot — 'torches'). Greek has λυχνίαι ('lampstands'). These are entirely different objects. A back-translator from Greek 'lampstands' would write מְנוֹרוֹת (menorot — 'menorahs/lampstands'), the standard Hebrew for Temple lampstands (Ex 25:31ff). The Hebrew author writes 'torches' — portable, outdoor flames evoking Gideon's torches (Judg 7:16,20) and night watchmen. The Greek translator converted the unfamiliar image to Temple furniture. This is one of the clearest one-way markers in the chapter: no translator from λυχνίαι would produce אבוקות.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'torches' (אבוקות). Greek: 'lampstands' (λυχνίαι). Completely different objects — portable outdoor flames vs. Temple furniture.

Hebrew: 'Elohim of the earth' (אלהי הארץ). Some Greek MSS have κυρίου ('Lord') while others have θεοῦ ('God'). The Zechariah 4:14 source has אֲדוֹן כָּל הָאָרֶץ ('the Lord of ALL the earth'). Neither Greek nor Hebrew Revelation preserves 'all' (כל), but the Hebrew uses a different divine title than the source.
translation_notes: אֲבוּקוֹת (avukot — 'torches') is a later Hebrew word not attested in the OT. No standard Strong's number. Its use here is natural Hebrew vocabulary, not a translation artifact.
'Olives' for zeitim — olive trees in Zechariah's vision supply oil for the lampstand. The Hebrew Revelation pairs olives with torches (oil-fed flames) rather than olives with lampstands.
textual_notes: Direct allusion to Zechariah 4:3,11-14 — the two olive trees standing beside 'the Lord of all the earth.' Zechariah's vision concerned Zerubbabel (royal) and Joshua (priestly) — the two anointed offices. The witnesses embody both royal and priestly authority.

verses.translation: And if anyone desires to do{H6213} them harm{H7451}, fire{H784} shall come{H935} and burn{H8313} them.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says simply 'fire shall come and burn them' (תבוא אש ושרף אותם) — fire arrives as divine judgment without specifying its source. Greek has πῦρ ἐκπορεύεται ἐκ τοῦ στόματος αὐτῶν ('fire proceeds out of their mouth'). The Greek adds the dramatic detail of fire issuing from the witnesses' mouths. The Hebrew presents fire as an external divine act — God sends fire, as with Elijah (2 Kings 1:10-12). A back-translator from Greek would include 'from their mouth' (מפיהם); its absence from the Hebrew is a one-way marker.

The Hebrew verse is a single concise statement. The Greek repeats the entire conditional clause and adds 'he must be killed in this way' (οὕτω δεῖ αὐτὸν ἀποκτανθῆναι). The Hebrew's brevity is characteristic of Hebrew prophetic style, not a condensation of Greek.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'fire comes out of their mouth and devours their enemies' (πῦρ ἐκπορεύεται ἐκ τοῦ στόματος αὐτῶν). Hebrew: 'fire shall come and burn them.' No mention of fire from mouths in the Hebrew.
Greek repeats the entire clause and adds a consequence: 'if anyone wants to harm them, he must be killed in this way.' Hebrew gives only one clause — far more concise.
translation_notes: רוֹצֶה (rotseh — 'desires/wants') is from the root רצה, which in the OT (H7521) carries connotations of delight, will, and acceptance (Ps 40:13, 51:16). Later Hebrew uses it as a general verb for 'want.'
'Burn' for saraf (H8313) — the same verb used for the burning of Sodom (Gen 19:24-25 uses a different verb, but saraf is used for divine burning throughout Leviticus).
textual_notes: 2 Kings 1:10-12 — Elijah called down fire from heaven on the captains who came against him. The fire imagery connects the witnesses to Elijah's prophetic authority.

verses.translation: And they have authority to shut{H5462} the heavens{H8064} so that rain{H1653} shall not come{H935} upon the earth{H776} in the days{H3117} of their prophesying{H5012}; and over the waters{H4325} to turn{H2015} them to blood{H1818}; and to strike{H5221} the earth{H776} with plagues{H5061} at every{H3605} season{H6256} they desire.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נְגָעִים (nega'im — 'plagues', H5061) — the specific Levitical term for divine afflictions: the plagues of Egypt (Ex 11:1) and priestly skin inspections (Lev 13-14). Greek πᾶσαν πληγήν ('every plague/blow') is more generic. A back-translator from Greek would likely use מַכּוֹת (makot — 'blows/strikes') or מגפה (magefah — 'plague'). The Hebrew author reaches for the Torah's technical Levitical term.

Uses לַהֲפֹךְ (lahafokh — 'to turn/overturn', H2015) for the water-to-blood transformation. This is the specific verb used for God's overturning of Sodom (Gen 19:21,25,29; Deut 29:23; Isa 13:19) and for the first Egyptian plague (Ex 7:17 — 'the water shall be turned to blood'). Greek στρέφειν is more neutral. The Hebrew verb carries overtones of catastrophic divine judgment beyond mere transformation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: רשות ('permission/authority') — a characteristically Mishnaic Hebrew word with no OT Strong's number. Greek: ἐξουσίαν ἔχουσιν ('they have authority'). The later Hebrew vocabulary is natural composition, not translation.
Hebrew: 'in the days of their prophesying' (בימי נבאיהם). Greek: 'in the days of their prophecy' (ταῖς ἡμέραις τῆς προφητείας αὐτῶν). Hebrew uses a verbal noun form; Greek uses the abstract noun.
translation_notes: 'Authority' for reshut — this Mishnaic Hebrew word carries the nuance of 'permission granted by a higher authority,' distinct from the more forceful Greek ἐξουσία. The witnesses act under divine license.
The threefold power structure — shutting heavens, turning water to blood, striking with plagues — combines the powers of Elijah (rain) and Moses (blood and plagues).
textual_notes: 1 Kings 17:1 — Elijah declared 'there shall be neither dew nor rain these years.' Exodus 7:17-20 — Moses turned water to blood. The witnesses exercise the combined authority of Israel's two greatest prophets.

verses.translation: And after they complete their testimony{H5715}, the beast{H2416} that goes{H1980} up from the Deep{H8415} shall make{H6213} war{H4421} against them and overcome{H5329} them and kill{H2026} them.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תְּהוֹם (tehom — 'the Deep', H8415) — the primordial chaos waters from Genesis 1:2 (וְחֹשֶׁךְ עַל־פְּנֵי תְהוֹם — 'and darkness upon the face of the Deep'). Greek has ἄβυσσος ('abyss'). While ἄβυσσος can correspond to tehom, the Hebrew word carries creation theology — the beast emerges from the pre-creation chaos, the unformed void that preceded God's ordering of the world. The OT resonances are far richer: Gen 1:2, 7:11, 8:2; Ps 42:7, 104:6; Isa 51:10. A back-translator might coincidentally use tehom, but the creation-theology dimension is uniquely Hebrew.

Uses עֵדוּתָם (edutam — 'their testimony', H5715). The root עדות (edut) is the specific Torah word for covenantal witness — the Ark is called אֲרוֹן הָעֵדוּת ('Ark of the Testimony', Ex 25:22), the Tabernacle is called מִשְׁכַּן הָעֵדוּת ('Dwelling-place of the Testimony', Ex 38:21). Greek μαρτυρία is broader. The Hebrew connects the witnesses' mission to Torah covenantal testimony.

Uses הַחַיָּה (ha-chayyah — 'the beast/living creature', H2416). This word means both 'living thing' (Gen 1:24, 2:19) and 'wild beast' (Gen 3:1, 37:20). It shares the root with חַיִּים ('life'). Greek θηρίον ('wild beast') is unambiguous. The Hebrew creates an ironic tension: the 'living thing' from the Deep brings death. A back-translator from Greek's unambiguous θηρίον would not stumble into this semantic layering.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: שֶׁהָלַךְ ('that went/goes', from הלך — 'walk'). Greek: τὸ ἀναβαῖνον ('the one ascending'). Hebrew uses the common motion verb; Greek uses the more dramatic 'ascending.' A back-translator from Greek would use עולה (oleh — 'ascending'), not הלך ('walking').
Hebrew: masculine verb הלך with feminine noun חיה — a gender mismatch characteristic of later Hebrew, not calqued from Greek where neuter θηρίον takes neuter participle.
translation_notes: Consonantal כלא (kala, H3607) means 'to shut up, restrain, withhold.' In context — 'after they shut up their testimony' — the sense is 'completed/concluded,' i.e., when their testimony reaches its appointed end. The consonantal root is כלא (with aleph), not כלה (H3615 — 'to finish'), though both converge in meaning here.
'The Deep' for tehom — preserving the Genesis creation connection. Not 'abyss' (a Greek loanword) or 'pit.'
textual_notes: Genesis 1:2 — the Deep (tehom) is the primordial chaos that preceded creation. The beast's origin in tehom marks it as an anti-creation force, emerging from the very chaos that God subdued at the beginning.

verses.translation: And their corpses{H5038} shall be cast{H2236} upon the plazas{H7339} of the holy{H6918} city{H5892}, which is called{H7121} Sodom{H5467} and Egypt{H4714}, because there our lord{H113} was crucified.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew calls Jerusalem הָעִיר הַקְּדוֹשָׁה ('the HOLY city', H6918). Greek calls it τῆς πόλεως τῆς μεγάλης ('the GREAT city'). Opposite characterizations. A back-translator from Greek 'great city' would write העיר הגדולה ('the great city'), not 'the holy city.' The Hebrew author maintains Jerusalem's sacred status even while comparing it to Sodom and Egypt — a profound theological tension that the Greek resolves by stripping the holiness designation. This is a major one-way marker.

Uses אֲדוֹנֵינוּ (adoneinu — 'OUR lord', H113, 1st person plural suffix). Greek has ὁ κύριος αὐτῶν ('THEIR Lord', 3rd person). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדוֹנֵיהֶם (adoneihem — 'their lord'), not אֲדוֹנֵינוּ ('our lord'). The Hebrew author includes himself among those who belong to the crucified lord — a first-person confession absent from the Greek.

Uses רְחוֹבוֹת (rechovot — 'plazas/broad places', H7339, PLURAL). Greek has τῆς πλατείας (singular 'street/plaza'). The Hebrew naturally pluralizes — a city has multiple public spaces. Same plural pattern appears in Rev 21:21.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the holy city' (העיר הקדושה). Greek: 'the great city' (τῆς πόλεως τῆς μεγάλης). Opposite characterization of Jerusalem.
Greek adds πνευματικῶς ('spiritually') — 'which is SPIRITUALLY called Sodom and Egypt.' Hebrew has simply 'which is called' (הנקרא) — no qualifier.
Hebrew: 'our lord' (אדונינו — 1st person). Greek: 'their Lord' (αὐτῶν — 3rd person). Different perspective.
Greek has singular πλατείας ('street'). Hebrew has plural רחובות ('plazas').
translation_notes: נִצְלַב (nitslav — 'was crucified') is from the root צלב, a native Hebrew/Aramaic verb attested in rabbinic literature. The Niphal conjugation is natural Hebrew grammar. No standard OT Strong's number since crucifixion was not an Israelite practice.
כֵּיוָן (keivan — 'because/since') is a later Hebrew conjunction not found in the OT. Its natural use here is characteristic of an author writing in post-Temple Hebrew, not translating from Greek.
textual_notes: Isaiah 1:10 — 'Hear the word of YHWH, you rulers of Sodom; give ear to the Torah of our God, you people of Gomorrah.' The prophet addresses Jerusalem's leaders as 'rulers of Sodom' while the city retains its identity as the place of YHWH's Torah. The Hebrew Revelation preserves this same tension — the city is simultaneously 'holy' and 'Sodom.'

verses.translation: And some from the peoples{H5971} and from the tribes{H7626} shall see{H7200} their corpses{H5038} three{H7969} days{H3117} and a half{H2677}, and they shall not bury{H6912} them.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew has TWO groups: 'peoples and tribes' (עמים ושבטים). Greek has FOUR: 'peoples and tribes and tongues and nations' (λαῶν καὶ φυλῶν καὶ γλωσσῶν καὶ ἐθνῶν). The four-part formula is a characteristic Revelation pattern in Greek (5:9, 7:9, 10:11, 13:7, 14:6). A back-translator working from Greek's standard four-part formula would include all four terms. The Hebrew author uses a simpler, more natural Hebrew pair.

Uses אֵיזֶה (eizeh — 'some/which ones'). This is a distinctly post-biblical Hebrew indefinite pronoun common in Mishnaic Hebrew. It has no Greek equivalent being translated — Greek uses βλέπουσιν ἐκ τῶν λαῶν ('they look from among the peoples'). The colloquial Hebrew eizeh is natural authorial vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Greek has four groups: peoples, tribes, tongues, nations. Hebrew has two: peoples, tribes.

Greek: 'shall not allow their dead bodies to be put into tombs' (οὐκ ἀφήσουσι τὰ πτώματα αὐτῶν τεθῆναι εἰς μνήματα). Hebrew: 'shall not bury them' (ולא תקברו אותם). Hebrew is far more concise; Greek specifies 'placed into tombs.'
translation_notes: The denial of burial is among the gravest dishonors in Israelite culture (1 Kings 14:11, Jer 7:33, 16:4, 22:19). The Hebrew reader understands the full weight of this horror.
textual_notes: Psalm 79:2-3 — 'They have given the dead bodies of your servants as food for the birds of the heavens, the flesh of your faithful to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them.' The unburied corpses echo the Psalm 79 lament over Jerusalem's desecration.

verses.translation: And those who dwell upon the earth{H776} shall rejoice{H8055} over them and send{H7971} gifts{H4979}, each man{H376} to his neighbor{H7453}, for [...] these prophets{H5030} made{H6213} much distress for those who dwell upon the earth{H776}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אִישׁ לְרֵעֵיהוּ (ish le-re'ehu — 'each man to his neighbor', H376+H7453). This is a fixed OT idiom appearing throughout the Tanakh (Ex 11:2, 32:27; Jer 31:34; Zech 3:10; Est 9:19,22). Greek has πέμψουσιν ἀλλήλοις ('they shall send to one another'). A back-translator from Greek's generic reciprocal would not produce this specific idiomatic pair. The Hebrew formulaic expression is too distinctive to derive from the Greek.

The text preserves a LACUNA: [  ] appears between כי and הנביאים. A manuscript gap exists in the source. This kind of scribal awareness — marking gaps rather than filling them — is characteristic of an original textual tradition, not a translation. A translator working from Greek would produce a seamless text; only a scribe copying from a damaged Hebrew original would preserve the gap.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'these two prophets tormented (ἐβασάνισαν) those dwelling on the earth.' Hebrew: 'these prophets made much distress (צער).' Greek implies active torture; Hebrew implies causing grief. Different severity.
Greek specifies 'two prophets' (δύο προφῆται). Hebrew says only 'these prophets' (הנביאים הללו) without the number.

Greek: 'they shall make merry and send gifts' (εὐφρανθήσονται... καὶ δῶρα πέμψουσιν). Hebrew: 'they shall rejoice and send gifts' (ישמחו... וישלחו מתנות). Similar but Hebrew שמח and Greek εὐφραίνω have different ranges of meaning.
translation_notes: אֵילּוּ (eilu — 'those') is a distinctly later Hebrew demonstrative pronoun, common in Mishnaic Hebrew. Its repeated use (vv. 10, 11) shows the author writes naturally in post-biblical idiom.
צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress/sorrow') is a later Hebrew word without a standard OT Strong's number. The root appears in Genesis 34:7 (עָצַב/עצר) but the noun form צער is Mishnaic.
'[...]' preserves the textual lacuna present in the Hebrew source.
textual_notes: The gift-sending echoes Esther 9:19,22 — the celebration of Purim, where Jews sent 'portions each man to his neighbor' (אִישׁ לְרֵעֵהוּ). The earth-dwellers' celebration over the prophets' deaths is a dark inversion of Purim — a festival of deliverance turned into a festival of murder.

verses.translation: And after three{H7969} days{H3117} and a half{H2677}, they arose{H6965} and stood upon their feet{H7272}, and great{H1419} dread{H6343} and terror{H367} fell{H5307} upon those who saw{H7200} them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פַּחַד וְאֵימָה (pachad ve-eimah — 'dread and terror', H6343+H367) with the verb נפל ('fell'). This EXACT combination echoes Exodus 15:16: תִּפֹּל עֲלֵיהֶם אֵימָתָה וָפַחַד — 'Terror and dread FALL upon them' — from the Song of the Sea describing the nations' fear at the Exodus. Greek has simply φόβος μέγας ('great fear' — one word). A back-translator from Greek's single word 'great fear' would write פחד גדול ('great fear') or יראה גדולה ('great fear'), NOT the specific Exodus 15:16 word-pair. The Hebrew author quotes the Song of the Sea; the Greek translator summarized it.

Hebrew says 'they arose and stood upon their feet' (קמים המה ודורסים על רגליהם) without explaining HOW they came back to life. Greek adds πνεῦμα ζωῆς ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ εἰσῆλθεν εἰς αὐτούς ('a spirit of life from God entered into them') — a theological explanation absent from the Hebrew. The Hebrew lets the miracle speak for itself; the Greek adds mechanism. A back-translator from Greek would include the 'spirit of life' detail.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'a spirit of life from God entered into them' (πνεῦμα ζωῆς ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ). Absent from Hebrew — the Hebrew simply says 'they arose.'
Greek: φόβος μέγας ('great fear' — single concept). Hebrew: פחד ואימה ('dread AND terror' — paired nouns from Exodus 15:16). The Hebrew is more specific and OT-rooted.
translation_notes: דוֹרְסִים (dorsim — 'treading/standing') is the same later Hebrew verb as in verse 2 (דרס). Here it means 'standing firmly' — treading on their own feet, i.e., standing upright.
'Dread and terror' preserves the Hebrew word-pair rather than collapsing it to 'great fear.'
textual_notes: Exodus 15:16 — 'Terror and dread fall upon them; by the greatness of your arm they are still as stone.' The nations' fear at the Exodus is re-enacted at the witnesses' resurrection.

Ezekiel 37:10 — 'And the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood upon their feet' (ויעמדו על רגליהם). The dry bones vision parallels the witnesses' resurrection. Note: the Greek Revelation may be drawing on Ezekiel's 'spirit/breath' language where the Hebrew Revelation does not.

verses.translation: And they heard{H8085} one{H259} voice{H6963} saying{H559} to them: Ascend{H5927}! And they ascended{H5927} upward{H4605} into the heavens{H8064} in one{H259} cloud{H6051}, and their enemies{H8130} saw{H7200} them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שׂוֹנְאֵיהֶם (son'eihem — 'their enemies/haters', from sane' H8130 — 'to hate'). Greek has ἐχθροὶ αὐτῶν ('their enemies'). A back-translator from Greek could use אוֹיְבֵיהֶם (oyveihem, from oyev — 'enemy') or צָרֵיהֶם (tsareihem, from tsar — 'adversary'). The choice of the 'hate' root (שנא) implies visceral personal hatred. This is the same root used of Esau's hatred (Gen 27:41) and the enemies in the Psalms (Ps 21:8, 34:21, 69:4). The vocabulary carries emotional, not political, enmity.

Uses בְּעָנָן אֶחָד ('in ONE cloud', H6051+H259 — numeral). Greek has ἐν τῇ νεφέλῃ ('in THE cloud' — definite article). Hebrew specifies 'one cloud' with the numeral; Greek uses the article. The Hebrew 'one cloud' connects to Daniel 7:13 (עִם עֲנָנֵי שְׁמַיָּא — 'with the clouds of heaven') and the pillar of cloud in the wilderness (Ex 13:21). A back-translator from Greek 'the cloud' would write בֶּעָנָן ('in the cloud') without the numeral.
greek_deviations: Greek: φωνὴ μεγάλη ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ('a great voice from heaven'). Hebrew: קול אחד ('one voice'). Hebrew has 'one' where Greek has 'great,' and 'from heaven' is absent from the Hebrew.
Greek: Ἀνάβατε ὧδε ('Come up HERE'). Hebrew: simply עלו ('Ascend!'). Hebrew is more concise — no destination specified.
translation_notes: 'Ascend' for alu — the verbal root עלה (alah, H5927) is the pilgrimage word: Israel 'goes up' to Jerusalem (Ps 122:4), offerings 'go up' on the altar. The witnesses' ascent is the ultimate aliyah.
'Enemies' for son'eihem — literally 'their haters,' preserving the emotional dimension.
textual_notes: 2 Kings 2:11 — Elijah ascended to heaven in a whirlwind. The witnesses' ascension in a cloud echoes both Elijah's departure and Yeshua's ascension (Acts 1:9 — 'a cloud received him out of their sight').

verses.translation: And in that hour there was a trembling of the earth{H776}, and a tenth{H6224} part{H2506} of the city{H5892} fell{H5307}, and seven{H7651} thousand{H505} of the sons{H1121} of Adam{H120} died{H4191}; and the rest{H312} were terrified{H926} and gave{H5414} praise to the Elohim{H430} of the heavens{H8064}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בְּנֵי אָדָם (benei adam — 'sons of Adam/mankind', H1121+H120). Greek has ὀνόματα ἀνθρώπων ('NAMES of men'). Hebrew counts 'sons of Adam' (living people); Greek counts 'names of men' (identities). A back-translator from Greek would write שְׁמוֹת אֲנָשִׁים ('names of men'), not the Hebrew collective expression בני אדם. The Hebrew phrase echoes the creation account — these are children of Adam who perish.

Uses שֶׁבַח (shebach — 'praise'). This is the specific Hebrew/Aramaic praise word from Daniel (Dan 2:23, 4:34). Greek has δόξαν ('glory'). A back-translator from Greek would use כָּבוֹד (kavod — 'glory'), not the Daniel-specific shebach. The Hebrew connects the survivors' response to Daniel's Babylonian-context praise.

Uses נִבְהֲלוּ (nivhalu — 'were terrified', Niphal of bahal H926). This is the exact verb used for Belshazzar's terror at the writing on the wall (Dan 5:9 — 'then King Belshazzar was greatly terrified/נִבְהַל'). Greek has ἔμφοβοι ἐγένοντο ('became fearful'). The Hebrew verb implies panicked, paralyzing terror — stronger than the Greek.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'seven thousand names of men' (ὀνόματα ἀνθρώπων). Hebrew: 'seven thousand of the sons of Adam' (מבני אדם). Different counting objects — names vs. people.
Greek: 'gave glory' (ἔδωκαν δόξαν). Hebrew: 'gave praise' (נתנו שבח). Different response — glory vs. praise.
Greek: ἔμφοβοι ('fearful'). Hebrew: נבהלו ('terrified'). Different intensity.
translation_notes: רַעֲדוֹת (ra'adot — 'tremblings') from the root רעד (H7460 — 'to tremble'). The plural form suggests repeated or rolling tremors, not a single cataclysmic quake. No exact OT Strong's for the plural noun form.
שָׁעָה (sha'ah — 'hour') is a later Hebrew word for a time unit, not the OT word. Its use here reflects natural post-biblical Hebrew.
textual_notes: 1 Kings 19:18 — YHWH reserved seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed to Baal. The seven thousand who die here may be a deliberate inverse echo: where Elijah's seven thousand were faithful survivors, these seven thousand perish. Both numbers are connected to the Elijah narrative that underlies the entire two-witnesses passage.

verses.translation: See{H7200}! The second{H8145} distress has gone{H1980}, and the third{H7992} comes{H935}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress/sorrow'). Greek has οὐαί ('woe' — an exclamation/interjection). A back-translator from Greek 'woe' would write הוֹי (hoy) — the standard OT prophetic interjection (Isa 5:8,11,18,20,21,22; Amos 5:18, 6:1). The Hebrew author chose a NOUN of suffering (distress), not a prophetic exclamation. These are different word classes entirely: a Greek exclamation cannot produce a Hebrew abstract noun.
greek_deviations: Greek: Ἡ οὐαὶ ἡ δευτέρα ('the second woe' — an exclamation). Hebrew: הצער השני ('the second distress' — a noun). Different word class and concept.
Greek adds ταχύ ('quickly') — 'the third woe comes QUICKLY.' Absent from the Hebrew. Hebrew is more concise.
translation_notes: צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress/sorrow') is a later Hebrew word without a standard OT Strong's number. It conveys inner grief and suffering, distinct from the externalized prophetic 'woe.'

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 11 in Hebrew presents the two witnesses passage with multiple layers of Torah, prophetic, and later Hebrew vocabulary that cannot derive from the Greek Textus Receptus. The chapter contains at least 15 clear one-way translation markers. The STRONGEST are: (1) 'torches' (אבוקות) vs. 'lampstands' (λυχνίαι) in v4 — completely different objects; (2) 'the INNER sanctuary' vs. 'the OUTER court' in v2 — opposite spatial references that no translator would reverse; (3) 'the HOLY city' vs. 'the GREAT city' in v8 — opposite characterizations of Jerusalem; (4) 'OUR lord' vs. 'THEIR Lord' in v8 — a person switch no translator would introduce; (5) the Exodus 15:16 dread-and-terror word-pair (פחד ואימה) in v11 — a specific OT quotation collapsed to 'great fear' in Greek; (6) the textual lacuna in v10 — a manuscript gap that only an original text tradition would preserve. The chapter is saturated with later Hebrew forms (אילו, רשות, כיון, צער, שעה, דרס) that indicate natural post-Temple Hebrew composition rather than translation. The witnesses combine the powers of Moses (blood, plagues) and Elijah (fire, drought, ascension), and the narrative is structured around Torah legal vocabulary: עדים (covenantal witnesses), עדות (covenantal testimony), תהום (the primordial Deep), and נגעים (Levitical plagues). The Hebrew and Greek diverge most dramatically on spatial theology (inner vs. outer sanctuary), the characterization of Jerusalem (holy vs. great), and the witnesses' instruments (torches vs. lampstands).
